newsitem.title: CHINA: China orders army, party out of futures trade.
newsitem.headline: China orders army, party out of futures trade.

text.p: China on Tuesday ordered the army to march out of the futures trade and take the ruling Communist Party with it.

The China Securities Regulatory Commission, the watchdog body for the securities and futures trade, barred futures brokers from accepting funds from the army, party and government unless they had permission from the State Council, or cabinet.
Brokers said the move, announced in the official China Securities newspaper, was aimed at stemming the haemorrhaging of state assets in the often casino-like futures trade.
"This ruling is clearly aimed at halting losses of state assets," said a senior executive at a futures trading house in the southern city of Shenzhen.
"The problem is that most of the futures trading houses were set up with investments from the state, the party or the army."
The ruling did not include any new measure to push the existing companies out of the trade.

Beijing has told the army to supplement its budget by going out and earning a living, and it has embraced the order with relish. Its investments span a wide range of business from hotels and bicycle factories to property and pharmaceuticals.
The Communist Party and many government agencies have also spent funds liberally in setting up firms or acquiring assets.
"This is part of a much larger problem," said a foreign diplomat who follows economic issues. "There is a wholesale loss of state assets that China wants to stop."
The securities watchdog body on Tuesday also announced annual inspections of all futures brokerages to ensure they had sufficient capital and were complying with trading regulations.
China has been trying to tame the "Wild West" atmosphere of its futures markets and keep them safely under some form of regulatory framework.

It was stunned by a series of multi-million dollar disputes in 1994 over currency and swap option contracts as well as metals trading overseas by what had been considered blue chip companies ranging from Minmetals International Non-Ferrous Metals Trading Co, Unipec and Sinochem to China international Trust and Investment Corp.
That prompted tighter rules over trading in a whole range of products overseas and renewed attention to the domestic market.
Regulators have slapped bans on contracts from oil to sugar and hounded hot money out of the market. In 1995, wild swings in treasury futures prompted a ban on the trade.
Last March, regulators banned securities brokers, trust companies and state firms from trading commodities futures and caps were imposed on daily price swings and position sizes.
That has taken much of the fun out of a market that still trades contracts drawn on plywood to red and green beans.

While trade in coffee and rubber on the southern Haikou exchange and green beans and wheat on the central Zhengzhou exchange has grown, most of China's 14 futures exchanges saw a sharp reduction in trading last year.

"We probably saw a fall in trading volume of some 40 to 50 percent last year from 1995 levels," said an official of the Beijing Commodity Exchange, which trades plywood and green beans and once was a big centre for treasury bill futures.
The Futures Herald said losses were incurred by 80 percent of the 330 specialised futures trading houses and some 2,500 firms that trade futures as one of their lines of businesses.
Regulators say market factors will finally force many exchanges out of business or into mergers with other markets.
